items.followUp: Define the octet rule and duplet rule, and give one example of an atom that follows each rule.

rubric.why: The octet rule describes the stable arrangement of eight electrons in an atom’s outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms tend to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell.

rubric.why: The duplet rule describes the stable arrangement of two electrons in the first shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that atoms tend to attain two electrons in their first shell.

modelAnswer: Octet rule: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to attain eight electrons in their outermost shell.
Duplet rule: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to attain two electrons in their first shell.

items.followUp: Define a single covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond consists of two pairs of electrons shared between atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two atoms share two pairs of electrons.

rubric.why: Oxygen and carbon dioxide contain double covalent bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as O₂ or CO₂.

modelAnswer: A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
Example: In an oxygen molecule, O=O, the two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom.
rubric.description: Identifies the hydrogen and electronegative atom involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attraction involving a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.description: Describes hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing attraction between molecules involving hydrogen.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular attractive force involving a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom.
It commonly occurs when hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen and is attracted to one of these atoms in a neighbouring molecule.

items.followUp: How does increasing temperature affect the rate of evaporation?

rubric.why: Strong intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules together and reduce their escape from the liquid.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of stronger intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that stronger intermolecular forces slow evaporation.

rubric.why: Weak intermolecular forces allow molecules to escape more easily, increasing evaporation.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of weaker intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that weaker intermolecular forces make evaporation faster.

modelAnswer: Strong intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules together, so fewer molecules escape and evaporation is slower.
Weak intermolecular forces allow molecules to escape more easily, so evaporation is faster.

items.followUp: Define a non-aqueous solution and give one example.

rubric.why: An aqueous solution is one in which water is the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is the solvent.

rubric.why: A correct example has a solute, such as salt or sugar, dissolved in water.
rubric.description: Gives one example of an aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a correct solute-in-water example.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a solution in which water is the solvent.
Example: Salt dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.
